extracted.intended_audience: psychological researchers studying humor and moral judgment
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria for when a situation will elicit humor according to the benign-violation hypothesis: the situation must be appraised as a violation, appraised as benign, and both appraisals must occur simultaneously; the page also enumerates mechanisms and moderators that make violations seem benign. Useful for researchers designing or evaluating humor stimuli or experiments in moral/humor psychology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Benign-violation hypothesis (overarching criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: The benign-violation hypothesis suggests that three conditions are jointly necessary and sufficient for eliciting humor: a situation must be appraised as a violation, a situation must be appraised as benign, and these two appraisals must occur simultaneously.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit statement from the paper; this is the core evaluative standard. Use as the primary test: a stimulus will be humorous only if it meets all three parts. Examples across studies and domains (moral violations, tickling, puns, slapstick) illustrate application. Anti-pattern: treating any single condition (e.g., mere incongruity) as sufficient without checking benignness or simultaneity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perceived violation (appraisal as a violation)
rubrics_metrics.description: A situation must be appraised as a violation — something that disrupts people’s sense of how the world ought to be (e.g., apparent threats, breaches of norms, taboo content).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Violations include physical threats (play fighting, tickling), personal-dignity violations (slapstick), linguistic violations (malapropisms, puns), social-norm breaches, and moral violations (bestiality, disrespect). Experimental manipulations contrast violation versus control versions (e.g., snorting ashes vs burying them) to ensure the stimulus is judged wrong. Anti-pattern: labeling an innocuous or purely mundane event as a violation without evidence that observers construe it as norm-violating.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perceived benignness (appraisal as benign)
rubrics_metrics.description: A situation must be appraised as benign — perceived as safe, playful, nonserious, or otherwise acceptable despite being a violation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Benignness can arise from harmlessness, playful context, alternative norms, weak commitment, or psychological distance. Examples: play fighting/tickling are mock threats construed as safe; a violation framed as hypothetical can seem benign. Anti-pattern: assuming psychological distance or alternative framing without operational manipulation; stimuli that are judged serious/real tend not to elicit humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simultaneity of appraisals (holding both appraisals at once)
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor requires that people simultaneously hold two contradictory interpretations of the same situation — that it is both a violation (wrong) and benign (not wrong/okay).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measured in studies by asking participants whether they can interpret a behavior as both "wrong" and "not wrong." Simultaneity mediates behavioral displays of amusement. Examples: puns require holding two meanings; a scenario that is both wrong (violates sexual norms) and acceptable under a harm-based norm can be amusing. Anti-pattern: sequential or exclusive appraisals (only seeing it as wrong or only as okay) do not produce the same amusement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternative/salient conflicting norm (one source of benignness)
rubrics_metrics.description: A violation may seem benign when one salient norm suggests the behavior is wrong while another salient norm suggests it is acceptable (conflicting norms).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: bestiality/necro­philia scenario may violate sexual norms but be acceptable under a harm-based norm if no one is harmed (dead chicken). Study 3 (kitten purring vs whining) shows harmlessness per an alternative norm increases amusement. Use conflicting-norm framing to increase benign appraisal. Anti-pattern: presenting only a single normative frame that makes the violation uniformly wrong.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weak commitment to the violated norm (another source of benignness)
rubrics_metrics.description: A violation may seem benign when observers are only weakly committed to the violated norm (low personal investment or identification with the norm).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: nonchurchgoers (low commitment) found a church raffling a Hummer more amusing than churchgoers (high commitment). Use individual-difference measures (attendance, endorsement) or select audiences with lower commitment to increase benign appraisal. Anti-pattern: assuming population-level acceptance — commitment varies and moderates amusement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Psychological distance (third source of benignness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Increasing psychological distance (temporal, social, spatial, likelihood, or hypotheticality) makes violations seem more benign and thus more likely to elicit amusement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study 5 primes far vs near distance; distant primes increased amusement for the chicken-sex scenario. Operationalize distance (prime tasks, hypothetical wording, temporal framing) to test or induce benignness. Anti-pattern: using stimuli that feel immediate/real or personally proximal, which reduce benignness and humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harmlessness vs harm as a moderator of benignness
rubrics_metrics.description: Actual or perceived harm to victims reduces benignness and therefore decreases amusement; harmless versions of violations produce more amusement and mixed emotions than harmful versions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study 3: kitten that purrs (harmless) elicits more amusement than kitten that is harmed. When behavior is wrong according to all relevant norms (harmful), amusement drops. When designing stimuli, ensure perceived lack of harm (or explicit statement of harmlessness) to increase humor likelihood.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mixed emotions as an indicator of benign violations
rubrics_metrics.description: Benign violations often produce mixed emotional responses: amusement and laughter can co-occur with negative emotions (especially disgust) rather than replacing them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Studies 3–5 documented higher rates of participants reporting both amusement and disgust for benign violations. Presence of mixed emotions (amused + disgusted) is diagnostic of benign moral violation humor. Anti-pattern: expecting humor to be purely positive; ignoring concurrent negative affect can miss key phenomenon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Behavioral and self-report measures for detecting amusement
rubrics_metrics.description: Amusement can be detected via behavioral displays (laughter, smiling) and self-report (did this scenario make you laugh? yes/no); observational coding by blind raters is recommended.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Studies used both observer-coded smiles/laughter and dichotomous self-report items. For mixed-emotion measurement, dichotomous yes/no items for amusement and disgust were used as recommended in mixed-emotion literature. Use multiple converging measures (behavioral observation + self-report) to assess amusement reliably.

rubrics_metrics.name: Domain-general applicability (types of violations that can be humorous when benign)
rubrics_metrics.description: The benign-violation framework applies across domains: tickling, teasing, slapstick, puns, linguistic and social norm violations, and moral violations can all be humorous when construed as benign violations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and theoretical discussion: tickling as mock attack, teasing as playful indirect provocation, slapstick as hypothetical harm, puns as language-convention violation with alternative interpretation. Use this criterion to generalize findings beyond moral scenarios; evaluate whether domain-specific features interact with benign-violation conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation-as-both-wrong-and-not-wrong mediates amusement
rubrics_metrics.description: The degree to which participants interpret a behavior as both wrong and not wrong partially mediates the relationship between violation framing and displays of amusement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical mediation evidence (Study 2, Baron & Kenny approach; Sobel test) suggests assessing simultaneity (both wrong & not wrong) can explain how manipulations produce laughter. For experimental designs include measures of dual-interpretation to test mediation.
